"Looking back at the 5 years, I don't know if I was able to reach the expectations that people had (for me) or for mys
item.content:encoded:
Ian Happ, Seiya Suzuki, Shota Imanaga sound like guys who won't be with Cubs much longer appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Chicago Cubs saw their season come to an abrupt conclusion Wednesday night when they lost their second consecutive game to the San Diego Padres in the Wild Card round of the National League playoffs.
"Looking back at the 5 years, I don't know if I was able to reach the expectations that people had (for me) or for myself."
Seiya Suzuki hit 113 home runs as a Cub in his first 5 MLB seasons, behind only Ernie Banks (136) and Kris Bryant (138). pic.twitter.com/rzxffiIVtX
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
— Marquee Sports Network (@WatchMarquee) October 1, 2026
The Cubs had a streaky regular season, often showing their dominance in the first half of the season with notable winning streaks, but they were unable to keep up with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NL Central. They finished in second place to the Brewers, a full 14.0 games behind Milwaukee. They didn't clinch their playoff spot until the final days of the regular season.
Chicago ended the year and entered the postseason as the No. 5 seed in the National League playoffs. They had to go on the road to play the Padres. That proved to be a big disadvantage, because the Padres were among the hottest teams in Major League Baseball as the postseason got underway.
There could be significant changes on the Cubs roster as the team prepares for the 2027 season. Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki, two veteran mainstays in the Cubs lineup, will be free agents in 2027 and it seems quite likely that both will be with new teams when the upcoming season gets underway.
Happ spoke in the locker room and it sounded like he was saying goodbye to the organization. "All I can say is that I love being a Cub," Happ said, per the Marquee Sports Network. "I've loved my time. I've loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fanbase. And it's been truly special. I don't think there's a better place in baseball to play."
Pitcher Shota Imanaga will also be a free agent in the offseason, and he may not figure in the team's pitching plans for the future.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Manny Machado Sends Clear Message After Padres' Sweep of Cubs
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: San Diego Padres star third baseman Manny Machado is ready for more after sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the wild-card series. Machado and the Padres defeated the Cubs in two games to advance to the National League Division Series. San Diego will now face the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers in a best-of-five series. Although San Diego will be the underdog in this upcoming series, Machado is poised to have three more champagne celebrations in October. “We’re not done,” Machado said in the postgame loc
item.content:encoded:
San Diego Padres star third baseman Manny Machado is ready for more after sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the wild-card series.
Machado and the Padres defeated the Cubs in two games to advance to the National League Division Series. San Diego will now face the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers in a best-of-five series.
Although San Diego will be the underdog in this upcoming series, Machado is poised to have three more champagne celebrations in October.
“We’re not done,” Machado said in the postgame locker room celebration. “We’re not done. We’re gonna continue to fight … to bring a championship to the city of San Diego.”
The Padres entered the 2026 postseason as one of the league's hottest teams, and they proved it in two games.
"Man, we've been playing some really good baseball," Machado said. "Hopefully we can keep doing that."
The Padres handled the Cubs in dominant fashion.
Chicago entered the series leading the majors in runs. However, they score just once in 18 innings and mustered only eight hits. The Padres dominated the Cubs in front of their home fans, and the pitching did their part.
Padres ace Michael King started things off with a bang. In Game 1 of the series, King led the way with seven scoreless innings.
Padres starter Nick Pivetta and the bullpen picked up right where King left off on Wednesday night.
"We do have a strong bullpen, and even the guys we haven't used are very good pitchers also," manager Craig Stammen said. "That's going to be the strength of our team as we go through the postseason."
Can the Padres Pull Off an Upset Against the Brewers?
The Padres enter their series against the Brewers as underdogs with +150 odds to come out on top.
The Brewers are major favorites with -180 odds.
Milwaukee enters with the best record in baseball. Likely NL Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski leads the Brewers in this series.
The young ace will likely get two starts if the series goes the distance.
While this will certainly be the Padres' toughest test yet, they are as confident as ever to get the job done.
"Momentum’s the biggest thing in baseball," Padres center fielder Jackson Merrill said. "It doesn’t matter whether it’s a regular-season game or a postseason game. Momentum is everything. We know they’re a good baseball team. They play the game to win.
"But you know what? We’re a pretty good baseball team, too."
Sign up for our free newsletter and follow us on Facebook and X/Twitter for the latest news.
Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

item.title: [chicago.suntimes.com] Stinging from playoff exit, Cubs must make sure next year is different: ‘It’s time to look in the mirror’
item.dc:creator: Vinnie Duber
item.description: SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville? It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs. They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals. Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October? They didn’t come close. “The goal is to win, and we didn’t play wel
item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

item.title: [reviewingthebrew.com] 3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by NLDS matchup with Padres, 2 reasons to be nervous

item.content:encoded:
After sweeping the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card Series, the San Diego Padres have officially punched their ticket to the NLDS, where a matchup with the top-seeded Milwaukee Brewers awaits them. It will be the Brewers and Padres' first-ever meeting in the postseason, and there are no two hotter teams in baseball right now. The Brewers and Padres each posted a 18-6 record during the regular season portion of their September schedule, and San Diego added two more convincing wins over the Cubs this week.
While Brewers fans are relieved not to have to deal with the added stress that comes with facing the Cubs in the postseason, the Padres' recent performance undoubtedly has some fans wishing for a matchup with Craig Counsell's squad. That said, for as well as the Padres are playing right now, there are still certainly reasons for Brewers fans to be encouraged by the specific matchup. Let's take a closer look at three of the Padres' weaknesses and how they might come into play in the NLDS.
3 reasons Brewers fans should be encouraged by their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. Question marks remain in San Diego's starting rotation
Heading into the postseason, the Padres' rotation was certainly their biggest weakness. With an elite bullpen and a surging offense, fans were unsure what San Diego would get from their starting staff in October. However, the duo of Michael King and Nick Pivetta, the latter of whom had a limited regular season workload this year due to an early-season elbow injury, dominated the Cubs in the Wild Card series, allowing just one earned run in a combined 10.1 innings. King's seven-inning shutout on Tuesday night did the heavy lifting, but Pivetta certainly impressed on Wednesday night as well.
However, even if King and Pivetta replicate their Wild Card performances in the NLDS -- likely in Games 2 and 3 -- questions remain in regard to the rest of San Diego's starting options. Trade deadline acquisitions Casey Mize, who is currently hurt, and Robbie Ray, who snuck onto the Wild Card roster but didn't pitch, haven't panned out as the Padres hoped they would. Long-time Los Angeles Dodger Walker Buehler also made the Padres' initial playoff roster, and is certainly a candidate to start a game, but his pedestrian 4.63 ERA in 32 starts this year doesn't necessarily scream "postseason starter." Not only will San Diego need King and Pivetta to repeat their incredible Wild Card performances in the NLDS, but they will also need another less obvious postseason starter to step up.
2. Padres' league-average infield defense bodes well for Brewers' offensive approach
The Cubs had an elite defensive unit in 2026, that much was obvious. In addition to Pete Crow-Armstrong's impressive performance in center field, the Cubs' infield of Alex Bregman (who was limited to DH in the Wild Card series due to a freak injury), Dansby Swanson, Nico Hoerner, and Michael Busch took away a number of would-be base hits thanks to their impressive range and sure-handedness. The Padres, while their infield unit is fine, by no means have the same elite ability to take away ground-ball base hits, and is therefore a better matchup for the Brewers' offense.
Manny Machado remains a strong defender when it comes to Outs Above Average (OAA), but his Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) total tells a different story. Ty France is a solid defensive first baseman, but the duo of Xander Bogaerts and Jake Cronenworth up the middle is below-average in the field. It's an important part of this series because the Brewers rank first in MLB in Batting Average on Balls in Play (BABIP), third in infield hits, and second in bunt hits. In other words, Milwaukee puts a lot of pressure on opposing infield defenses, and the Padres' shaky unit could come back to hurt them in this series.
3. San Diego's offense was far closer to league average for a majority of the season
The Padres' offense is on fire right now. No team posted a higher collective batting average, slugging percentage, or wRC+ than the Padres during the month of September, and only the Brewers scored more runs. Strong final months from Fernando Tatis Jr., Jackson Merrill, France, and Bogaerts led the Padres to these impressive numbers during the month of September, but for a majority of the season, San Diego's offense looked far closer to league average.
From the start of the season to the end of August, San Diego held a collective wRC+ of 98, indicating that their offensive unit was below league average for the first five months of the season. During that stretch, they ranked 20th in home runs and 22nd in runs scored. Their strong final push made their season-long numbers appear far better, but for a majority of the 2026 season, San Diego's offense was not among the best in baseball. That could matter not if the Padres' recent hot streak continues throughout October, but it's important to note this recent performance is the exception, not the norm.
2 reasons Brewers fans should be nervous about their NLDS matchup with the Padres
1. The Padres are the hottest team in baseball (aside from maybe the Brewers)
Whether their recent performance is the exception or not, there's no denying that the Padres are one of the two hottest teams in baseball, with their only threat being the team they will match up against in the NLDS. As previously mentioned, the Brewers and Padres finished first and second, respectively, in runs scored during the final month of the regular season en route to MLB-best 18-6 records. The Padres then stymied a strong Cubs' team with two comfortable wins in the NL Wild Card Series.
For the Brewers, who seemingly run into the hottest team in baseball in the early rounds of the postseason every single year, a matchup with the Padres feels like more bad luck. San Diego surged to the top Wild Card spot in the NL, secured a home postseason series, swept said series, and now carries that momentum into the NLDS. That certainly doesn't feel like a fair draw for the best team in baseball, who just completed a record-breaking 103-win regular season. Yes, the Padres have more flaws on their roster than the Brewers, but sometimes all that matters is how a team is playing when the postseason rolls around, to which the recent performance of each of these two teams would suggest fans are in for a competitive series.
2. San Diego is the only team with a better bullpen than the Brewers
The Brewers are heading into the postseason with their bullpen at its best, which is not often the case following the 162-game season. The combination of Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby at the back end, trade deadline acquisitions JoJo Romero and Antonio Senzatela in the middle innings, and multi-inning options like DL Hall, Chad Patrick, and Shane Drohan has Milwaukee's relief corps among the best in baseball as the playoffs arrive.
However, if there's one bullpen group that is better than the Brewers', it's the Padres' ridiculous assembly of relief weapons. Flame-throwing closer Mason Miller and his elite set-up man Adrian Morejon rightfully garner much of the attention, but other arms like Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, who just returned from the 60-day IL, and southpaw Yuki Matsui deserve respect as well. Given the strength of San Diego's bullpen and the question marks in their rotation, the pressure will be on the Brewers to build early leads and take advantage of as many scoring opportunities as possible.

item.content:encoded:
In 1969, the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers — who were the Seattle Pilots for one season — were founded as MLB expansion teams.
Now, 58 short years later, the perennial National League contenders are meeting in the postseason for the first time.
On Saturday, Oct. 3, the best-of-five NLDS will get underway at Milwaukee’s American Family Field with the Brewers’ ace and Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski (16-5, 1.80 ERA) on the hill.
Following a two-game stint in the Cream City, the series will move to SoCal for a pair of contests at San Diego’s PETCO Park. They’re slated to take place:
Game 3
Tuesday, Oct. 6
Game 4
Wednesday, Oct. 7
If you’d like to be there, tickets are available for both high-stakes hypothetical San Diego showdowns.
At the time of publication, the lowest price we could find on tickets for either game was $121 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $99 including fees for the three potential meetings in Milwaukee.
Before this series, the Padres got revenge against the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card round, sweeping MVP hopeful Pete Crow-Armstrong’s club at home after losing to them in three games to open the playoffs last year.
“They’re playing great baseball right now,” San Diego manager Craig Stammen said about his club.
Next up, they have a tall task taking on MLB’s winningest team in 2026.
Oddsmakers project the Brewers are -180 favorites going into the NLDS.
Yet, it should be factored in that San Diego took four of their six meetings over the course of the regular season including a clutch 4-3, eleven-inning victory on Aug. 12.
Is this the year that one of these two clubs finally gets over the hump and returns to the World Series?
While we can’t say for certain we do know that their first-ever postseason meeting with some of the game’s hardest flamethrowers in Misiorowski and Mason Miller should be downright electric.
Don’t miss this one. We just might have an instant classic on our hands.
For more information, our team has everything you need to know and more about the Padres vs. Brewers 2026 NLDS below.

Starry-eyed fans looking to get ahead of themselves can procure potential NLCS and World Series tickets before the NLDS even begins.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] “I Don’t Want to Give My Honest Answer” – Willson Contreras Gets Real About Red Sox Issues After Yankees Send Them Out of Wild Card
item.dc:creator: Nancy Singh
item.description: Willson Contreras shared his honest take on the Boston Red Sox's shortcomings after their Wild Card sweep by the New York Yankees, pointing to areas the team must improve. The Red Sox were eliminated from the 2026 MLB postseason after the Yankees swept them 2-0 in the American League Wild Card Series. item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras shared his honest take on the Boston Red Sox's shortcomings after their Wild Card sweep by the New York Yankees, pointing to areas the team must improve.
The Red Sox were eliminated from the 2026 MLB postseason after the Yankees swept them 2-0 in the American League Wild Card Series. The Yankees dominated the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium, outscoring Boston 18-2 across the two games. In Game 1, the Yankees shut out Boston 9-0 behind a strong performance from Cam Schlittler, who threw 6.1 scoreless innings.
In Game 2, Max Fried dominated for six innings before the Red Sox briefly found some momentum when Contreras hit a solo home run in the sixth inning, snapping Boston's 26-inning postseason scoring drought. However, the Yankees quickly regained control and eventually secured a 9-2 victory to complete the sweep. Following the loss, Contreras shared his honest response during the postgame locker room interview.
When asked about what went wrong with the Red Sox offense down the stretch of the regular season and into the playoffs, he said:
"I'm not gonna answer it because, I don't wanna give my honest answer, but, we got eliminated, that's the bottom line. We got in here trying to win. We didn't produce, we didn't execute any part of the game, and that's why we lose. I mean, I know that we had a really good stretch," said Willson Contreras.
He added:
"I'm really proud of what we did in the past, like I said, we were able to turn the season around for sure, 100%, but that's not enough. It's not enough, and at the end of the day, you win games in the regular season to clinch the playoffs, but then falling short in the playoffs, it's tough."
Despite the disappointing ending, the 2026 season was a rollercoaster for Boston. After a 32-46 start that left them at the bottom of the AL, the team went on a historic second-half surge to secure a playoff berth.
What did Willson Contreras say after the Red Sox clinched a spot in the 2026 playoffs?
The Boston Red Sox clinched an American League Wild Card spot in the 2026 MLB playoffs on Sept. 20. Despite losing 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays, they secured a postseason berth after the Atlanta Braves defeated the Houston Astros. The Astros' loss officially eliminated them from contention and secured Boston's playoff spot.
Following the achievement, Willson Contreras reflected on the team's remarkable turnaround in an interview. Expressing his pride in the team and his belief in his teammates, he said:
"I'm really thankful, first of all, for playing for Boston. Thankful for the front office for asking me to come here and all of the good human beings that are here on this team. This is just the first step ahead. I just wanted to let everybody know that I'm proud of every one of you," said Willson Contreras.
He added:
"I did believe in my team. I did believe in everybody who was here. I never had a doubt that this team couldn't turn the season around. At one point, we were texting each other and I just said, 'Keep believing in ourselves.'"
Contreras played as a first baseman and designated hitter for the Red Sox in 2026, setting career highs in home runs and RBIs. He played 130 games during the regular season, recording 123 hits and 68 runs.

While the Braves have welcomed star outfielder Ro
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 30: Ronald Acuña Jr. #13 of the Atlanta Braves reacts after scoring against the Philadelphia Phillies during the first inning in game two of the National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park on September 30, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)
There is a big time MLB playoff matchup on the National League side of the bracket on Thursday between the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
While the Braves have welcomed star outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr.’s services through the first two games of the season, some spectators and patrons don’t believe he’s been very productive and are calling on him to have a signature moment on Thursday evening.
Across the first two games of the Wild Card series with the Phillies, Ronald Acuña Jr. is 0-for-6 with a run scored, two stolen bases, and two walks.
Being that he’s either going to be the Braves’ first or second batter when manager Walt Weiss reveals the team’s lineup, it’s understandable why Atlanta might need more from the top of their order.
Ronald Acuña Jr. Could Be Difference Maker in Phillies-Braves Game 3 of WC
Atlanta Braves fans are calling on Ronald Acuña Jr. to have a signature moment in game three of the team’s Wild Card matchup with the Philadelphia Phillies.
Here are some reactions across Braves Country on socials:
@StatsSAC: “It has been nearly 6 years and over 80 plate appearances since Acuna Jr. hit a postseason home run If you wanna talk about due, it’s Ronald And him being the superstar he is is best path to winning this series and having some sort of hope vs Dodgers”
Aaron Nola is set to start the game for the Phillies, and Acuña Jr. has had a lot of success off the right-hander.
@HammerTerritory: “The Braves haven’t won an elimination game since Ronald Acuña Jr.’s ROOKIE season.”
Even Braves reporter Mark Bowman got into the conversation about RAJ:
“Ronald Acuna Jr. had his fun with Phillies fans in September, but he has hit .200 (7-for-36) with 2XBHs (both doubles), a .606 OPS, nine strikeouts and five walks in 10 postseason games vs. Philly going back to 2022. He’s 0-for-6 w/ 2BB and 2Ks during the current series.”
It would be a huge boost for the Braves if Ronald Acuña Jr. could come up with a huge swing against whoever is pitching for Philly.
TJ French covers the MLB for Heavy. TJ is a graduate of the University of Georgia. He has 2+ years of writing experience.

item.title: [MLB.com] Lights-out bullpen deployed to perfection in Padres' Wild Card Series clinch
item.dc:creator: Cole Bradley
item.description: SAN DIEGO -- The lights cut out, Korn’s “Blind” blared, the sellout Petco Park crowd rose to their feet roaring and Mason Miller seemingly spawned onto the mound for the start of the ninth inning. The game was over. The National League Wild Card Series was over. But in reality, it had ended well before that. This is exactly why Padres general manager A.J. item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO -- The lights cut out, Korn’s “Blind” blared, the sellout Petco Park crowd rose to their feet roaring and Mason Miller seemingly spawned onto the mound for the start of the ninth inning. The game was over. The National League Wild Card Series was over.
But in reality, it had ended well before that.
This is exactly why Padres general manager A.J. Preller assembled the best and deepest bullpen in baseball, for nights like Wednesday.
“In the postseason, you’ve got to get a lot of great hitters out,” Preller said. “You’ve got to have a lot of answers in that bullpen.”
After starter Nick Pivetta departed in the fourth, Padres manager Craig Stammen fully unleashed his bullpen over the final 5 2/3 innings against the Cubs in Game 2. Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, Adrian Morejon and Miller proceeded to allow just three men to reach base and keep Chicago’s league-best offense scoreless to slam the door on a 4-1 victory and send the Padres to the NL Division Series for a best-of-five-series against the Brewers.
Michael King going seven scoreless innings in Game 1 and saving the key arms in the back end set the Padres up perfectly to lean on that group the following night. If the Padres got an early lead, Stammen wasn’t going to mess around with keeping Pivetta in longer than he needed to secure the series.
That’s exactly how things played out.
San Diego scored a pair of runs in the second before Pivetta -- who did his job in limiting the Cubs over 3 1/3 innings -- got the hook in the fourth after giving up an RBI single to Nico Hoerner. A one-run lead ballooned to three after Gavin Sheets’ pinch-hit homer in the bottom half of the inning. The ‘pen took care of the rest.
“Michael’s effort last night was phenomenal and that allows us to go out firing in the early part of the game today and get our best guys out there,” Miller said. “It puts us in a really confident position. We get a lead and we feel really good about it.”
Perhaps the most important aspect of the Padres’ performance in this series was shutting down the Cubs’ elite lineup, and specifically their top two hitters in Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman. The former is coming off the seventh 40-40 season in baseball history and the latter posted a 1.010 OPS in the second half.
They collectively went 0-for-15 in the series with eight strikeouts.
It was quite the statement, but it’s exactly what the Padres have been doing all season. By innings, San Diego had the fourth-most used bullpen in the Majors (683 2/3) and it possessed the fifth-best ERA (3.53).
“It’s an incredible group, top to bottom,” Adam said. “It doesn’t matter the situation, it doesn’t matter the inning, everybody out there is ready to go at all times. Fourth inning, ninth inning, I don’t care who we put out there, I feel really confident the guy is getting the job done.”
Rodriguez was the first into the fray, the rookie right-hander who immediately became one of the best relief arms in the sport and has been dominant in high-leverage situations throughout the year. He played fireman in the fourth, escaping a bases-loaded jam to preserve Pivetta’s line before pitching a clean fifth that he capped with a strikeout of Seiya Suzuki on a changeup below the zone.
“We’ve always known that about Bradgley -- that his maturity level is beyond his years,” Padres pitching coach Ruben Niebla said. “He doesn’t rattle. He doesn’t get nervous. He trusts himself and is a confident guy. We’re able to put him in those situations very confidently, and he’s responded well to that.”
Adam got through a 1-2-3 sixth, then Morejon cruised through the seventh and eighth, allowing just one hit, a Tyrone Taylor single. Then the ball was handed to Miller, the most imposing reliever in the game, who struck out an insane 47.4% of the batters he faced this season and finished with a career-best 1.67 ERA and 38 saves.
He gave up a double to Hoerner but struck out a pair and got Carson Kelly to ground out to end it, sending the Padres to Milwaukee and the Cubs back home.
“It’s not about any individual, it’s about a group,” Miller said. “It’s about passing the ball to the next guy and getting us in the clubhouse with a win. I think it’s a lot of selfless guys down there.”
Now, the Padres get the top-seeded Brewers in the NLDS, another team with plenty of firepower in the bullpen. To defeat them, and anyone else standing in the Padres’ way this October, Wednesday will be the template.
And if it continues to pan out the way it did, that should scare the rest of the postseason field.
“We knew we had six innings we could cover,” Niebla said. “It worked out to perfection.”

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] MLB Playoff Roundup: Alec Bohm’s 10th-inning homer forces Game 3 against Braves
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa. The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the post
item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves will host the Philadelphia Phillies in a decisive Game Three of the National League Wild Card series tonight (Thursday, October 1). The winner will advance to face the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Division Series (NLDS). The Braves won Game One, but the Phillies rallied to win Game Two on Wednesday (September 30), setting the stage for this winner-take-all contest.
The game will start at 8 p.m. ET and will be broadcast on NBC and Peacock. Spanish language coverage will be available on Universo and Univision Radio, while ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games.
The Phillies' starting pitcher remains undecided, with options including Aaron Nola and ace Zack Wheeler. Meanwhile, the Braves may rely on Grant Holmes to handle the bulk of the innings, though they have not confirmed if he will start or follow an opener. Left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter are potential openers.
Both teams have key players to watch. For the Phillies, Alec Bohm hit a game-winning homer in Game Two, while Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber hit back-to-back homers in the eighth inning to tie the game. On the Braves' side, Michael Harris II and Mauricio Dubón have been performing well at the plate.
The Phillies have a history of postseason success against the Braves, having defeated them in previous playoff series, including the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS. The outcome of tonight's game will determine who advances to face the Dodgers in the next round.

item.title: [mix1063.com] White Sox pounce early, finish sweep of Astros for first playoff series win since 2005 | Mix 106.3 – Jonesboro, AR
item.description: By KRISTIE RIEKEN AP Sports Writer HOUSTON (AP) — From 100 losses to their first playoff series win in two decades, these scrappy Chicago White Sox just keep outdoing themselves. The White Sox used a big first inning and a three-run homer from Chase Meidroth to propel them to a 7-3 win over the Houston Astros on Wednesday to sweep their AL Wild Card Series. “I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them as they’re probably the only ones in this country that believed that they could be in th
item.content:encoded:
By KRISTIE RIEKEN AP Sports Writer
HOUSTON (AP) — From 100 losses to their first playoff series win in two decades, these scrappy Chicago White Sox just keep outdoing themselves.
The White Sox used a big first inning and a three-run homer from Chase Meidroth to propel them to a 7-3 win over the Houston Astros on Wednesday to sweep their AL Wild Card Series.
“I’m proud of the guys and certainly happy for them as they’re probably the only ones in this country that believed that they could be in this spot,” manager Will Venable said. “And they maintained that belief in the beginning of the season and went throughout the season maintaining that, and they made it happen. So it’s awesome to get to this point.”
It’s the first time Chicago has won a playoff series since beating Houston in the World Series in 2005. Under the direction of Venable, the second-year skipper, and with a letter of support from Pope Leo XIV, the White Sox advanced to face AL Central champion Cleveland in the AL Division Series beginning Saturday in Cleveland.
“It means everything for our fans,” Meidroth said. “They have been incredible all year. So the main thing was getting back to Chicago for some postseason baseball, and so we’re really blessed that we get to do that.”
The White Sox, who lost 100 games in each of the last three seasons, are the only team in major league history to follow consecutive 100-loss seasons with a playoff berth.
The AL West-winning Astros went 81-81 to become the first team to reach the postseason without a winning record. Their recent playoff woes in Houston continued Wednesday as they dropped their ninth straight home playoff game in a ninth trip to the postseason in the last 10 years.
Chicago pounced on the Astros for four runs in the first inning a day after scoring three in the first two innings of a 6-3 win. Houston ace Hunter Brown was lifted after getting just two outs and wasn’t helped by a sloppy defense which committed two first-inning errors.
He was 6-0 with a 2.39 ERA in six career starts against the White Sox before Wednesday’s debacle.
The Astros clawed their way back into it with solo home runs from Jeremy Peña, Cam Smith and Jose Altuve to trail by 1 entering the sixth inning.
AJ Blubaugh, who opened Game 1, and Peter Lambert, pitching on two days’ rest, combined to retire the next 13 batters after Brown exited. Chicago’s next baserunner came when Lambert walked Andrew Benintendi to start the sixth and then walked Tristan Peters.
Bryan Abreu came in, and Meidroth smashed his fifth pitch off the wall in left field to push the lead to 7-3. He yelled on his entire trip around the bases to the delight of a patch of White Sox fans seated near the visitor’s dugout.
“I was looking for something middle up,” Meidroth said. “He’s had my number all year, really good fastball, so I got something middle up and I was able to cash in for the team. So, yeah, that was awesome.”
Houston faced boos for a second game in a row from an unusually thin crowd. It’s a second straight playoff trip where the Astros have been swept at home in the wild card after losing both games to Detroit in 2024.
Now they’ll face an uncertain future with manager Joe Espada’s contract set to expire at season’s end after general manager Dana Brown was fired last month.
“We fought back and we set our goal to win this division and we accomplished that,” Espada said. “We wanted to play deep in October. We came short on that. But just the way our guys stayed together and were able to get this far, extremely proud of our team.”
It was a disappointing series for Houston slugger and AL MVP-favorite Yordan Alvarez, who managed only a single with two strikeouts in eight at-bats in the series.
Altuve’s shot to the seats in left field in the fourth inning got the Astros within 4-3. It was the 28th postseason homer of his career, which is second in MLB history behind Manny Ramirez (29).
“We’re all sad,” Altuve said. “We wanted to go to the World Series and win it. But today is sorrow for the final day of the season.”
The Astros had a shot to take the lead before Meidroth’s homer. They loaded the bases with two outs in the fifth, but Anthony Kay retired Altuve on a fly out to end the inning.
___

item.title: [phillyvoice.com] 5 thoughts about the Phillies: Aaron Nola's start, Alec Bohm's bomb and making history
item.dc:creator: Evan Macy PhillyVoice Staff
item.description: October 01, 2026 It feels sort of unexpected, that the Phillies are not only alive, but have some momentum with the third and final game of the NL Wild Card Series in Atlanta set for Thursday night. Just one win, and the Phillies can hop on a flight to Los Angeles to try and get revenge against the Dodgers for last season's NLDS failure. item.content:encoded:
October 01, 2026
It feels sort of unexpected, that the Phillies are not only alive, but have some momentum with the third and final game of the NL Wild Card Series in Atlanta set for Thursday night.
Just one win, and the Phillies can hop on a flight to Los Angeles to try and get revenge against the Dodgers for last season's NLDS failure.
Before Game 3's first pitch, we have a few Phillies' thoughts we'd like to share:
How are we feeling about Aaron Nola — named Game 3's starter earlier Thursday morning? In his 15 starts prior to last Saturday's bizarre three run first inning and out for the Phillies' veteran, Nola boasted a pretty solid 3.12 ERA which is more in line with the Nola who got a monster free agent contract a few offseasons ago.
He's also got some postseason pedigree. He's started 11 playoff games over the last five Octobers, and his two worst starts actually came during the World Series run in 2022. In six starts since 2023, he has a 3.00 ERA and 3-2 record. Is he better than Zack Wheeler pitching on three days rest for the first time ever? The Phils coaching staff made their choice and it's a reasonable one, if nothing else.
If Alec Bohm is parting ways with the Phillies in a few weeks — his contract is set to expire and the Phillies are likely to let him walk and give top prospect Aidan Miller the chance to start the season at third (or second) in 2027 — he gave Phillies fans a spectacular parting gift.
ALEC BOHM GO-AHEAD HOMER
PHILLIES LEAD IN THE 10TH 🤯 pic.twitter.com/S4wFOFyDq1
By virtue of all three other Wild Card series' wrapping up (more on that in a second), the Phillies have Thursday all to themselves and have moved from a 2 p.m. start to prime time (at 8:15 on NBC).
The Phillies are no strangers to primetime playoff starts — they've had a ton of them over the last half decade. They also play better at night. Their win percentage under the lights (55.5%, 61-49) is better than during the afternoon (51%, 26-25). With some extra time for their pitchers to rest and prepare, this is probably a net positive move for the Phillies.
As we just mentioned, the other three series' ended with a 2-0 sweep. Since the league switched to the three-game Wild Card first round format, teams who win Game 1 are now 24-3. The Phillies have a chance to be the fourth.
Philadelphia also has the chance to be the first team in franchise history to win a playoff series (albeit a short one) after losing a Game 1. They are 0-9 historically when they start a series off with a loss.
Another mark, probably, in the Phillies' advantage column is that they're going up against a Braves team unprepared to send a third starter out there. Lefty reliever Ray Kerr — with an impressive 1.77 ERA this season — is going to start the game, likely to face the lefty-heavy front of the Phillies order (Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber). Perhaps the Phillies should consider splitting these hitters up and having Schwarber bat lead off, with Trea Turner second and Harper third?
After Kerr, it's expected the Braves will go to righty starter Grant Holmes, who has a 3.44 ERA this season. Holmes faced the Phillies four times during the regular season and the Phils' hitters will all have recent recollections of facing him.
The Phillies will see how far they can get behind Nola, but it'll be interesting to see who's the next man in. Will it be Jesús Luzardo who pitched in Game 1? Will they ultimately call on Wheeler (or optimistically save him for an NLDS Game 1)? Can Andrew Painter throw on back-to-back days?

item.description: Whenever a baseball team wins a postseason series and celebrates with champagne and drinks in the locker room, it seems like reporters are just as much a part of the party as the players. And who wouldn’t want to celebrate with John Fanta? The San Diego Padres were the last team to celebrate late Wednesday night, sweeping the Chicago Cubs in two games to win their Wild Card series. And much like we saw in Chicago with the White Sox and in New York with the Yankees, there were festive scenes. And
item.content:encoded:
Whenever a baseball team wins a postseason series and celebrates with champagne and drinks in the locker room, it seems like reporters are just as much a part of the party as the players. And who wouldn’t want to celebrate with John Fanta?
The San Diego Padres were the last team to celebrate late Wednesday night, sweeping the Chicago Cubs in two games to win their Wild Card series. And much like we saw in Chicago with the White Sox and in New York with the Yankees, there were festive scenes. And while nobody quite did it like Muretaka Murakami with the South Siders, the Padres at least had NBC’s energetic and affable reporter/host/announcer in their clubhouse.
Fanta interviewed Padres superstar Fernando Tatis Jr. in the locker room and asked about how the team found their groove after a mediocre first 100 games of the season. He also asked Tatis to look ahead to the challenge of facing the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS and ace pitcher Jacob Misiorowski.
But honestly, all we wanted to see was John Fanta get doused with some kind of alcoholic beverage. And that’s what Tatis delivered. A bottle of Bud Light was the shower of choice. Thankfully, Fanta was wearing a clear plastic parka because he knew what was coming, too.
A conversation and a Bud Light shower with Fernando Tatis Jr.
The San Diego Padres are rolling on to Milwaukee. pic.twitter.com/LVyKbvxvIS
— John Fanta (@John_Fanta) October 1, 2026
We have certainly come a long way since the days when Tim McCarver and Deion Sanders shared a tense moment with the Atlanta Braves all those years ago, when he got his own bath in the locker room.

item.content:encoded:
Phillies' Aaron Nola Reportedly Starting vs. Braves over Zack Wheeler For MLB Playoffs Series Finale
The Philadelphia Phillies will go into Thursday's winner-take-all Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card series with Aaron Nola starting on the mound.
Per The Athletic's Matt Gelb, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly is going with Nola rather than using Zack Wheeler on short rest with a spot in the NLDS at stake.
As a result of their four-game losing streak last week that prevented them from clinching a playoff spot early, the Phillies had to use Wheeler on the final day of the regular season.
Wheeler allowed one run over six innings in a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays to help Philadelphia secure its postseason berth, but the situation left his status for the wild card round unclear.
Even though Wheeler won't get the start, Mattingly told reporters after Wednesday's 4-3 win to extend the series "it'll be pretty much all hands on deck" for Game 3.
The Phillies are fortunate to have a deep starting staff that allowed them to go with All-Stars Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez in the first two games against Atlanta.
However, Game 3 left Mattingly with a decision between Nola or Wheeler. John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia noted Wheeler has never started a game in the regular season or playoffs on short rest.
Wheeler's only relief appearance in his MLB career was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS against the Arizona Diamondbacks. He tossed 1.2 scoreless innings in a 9-7 loss.
Nola will be pitching on regular rest after starting on Saturday against the Rays. He only made it through one inning, allowing three runs on four hits in a 12-1 loss.
While Nola's overall stat line this season doesn't look great with a 4.67 ERA, he did get better as the year went on. The right-hander had a 3.33 ERA in 14 starts after the All-Star break.
Nola made three starts against Atlanta this season with two coming in a five-day span from Sept. 6-11. He allowed three runs and struck out eight over 13.1 innings in those two outings last month.
The Phillies forced Game 3 against Atlanta thanks to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hitting back-to-back homers in the eighth to tie the score at three. Alec Bohm delivered the go-ahead solo homer in the top of the 10th.
Andrew Painter finished the game on the mound with three scoreless innings out of the bullpen.
Game 3 between the Phillies and Braves from Truist Park will be played at 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. The winner will advance to play the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS starting on Saturday.

item.content:encoded:
San Diego stayed hot against the Cubs in the wild-card series, sweeping Chicago in two games to advance. The Padres clubhouse, naturally, was full of celebrations — including one featuring owner Kwanza Jones and Fernando Tatis Jr.
Jones celebrated with the players following the team’s victory over Chicago, wearing ski goggles and popping bottles of champagne.
Jones, and her husband, Jose E. Feliciano purchased the Padres for $3.9 billion from the Seidler family in August.
The couple held an official introductory press conference at the end of August, where Jones promised the team would “win it all” in the foreseeable future. Thus far, the Padres have come out roaring in the postseason.
San Diego scored 12 runs in two games against the Cubs, while the Padres pitching staff limited Chicago to a single run throughout the wild-card series.
“It’s another step,” Jones said. “It’s not the end of the journey it’s a continuation.”
The next step for San Diego will be facing the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers. If the Padres bats stay hot and the pitching staff remains sharp, there’s a good chance the rest of the playoffs run through San Diego.

item.content:encoded:
MLB playoff schedule 2026: Full bracket, scores, times, TV channels to watch every postseason series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
More than seven months after pitchers and catchers reported to spring training, it's time to determine which team will wear the MLB crown in 2026.
Twelve teams reached the postseason bracket, and any discussion about favorites has to start with the two-time defending champion Dodgers. Los Angeles wasn't necessarily dominant during the regular season and enters October with concerns about the health of the planet's best player, Shohei Ohtani, but it has proven unwise to bet against LA lately.
While the Dodgers are in the midst of a dynastic run, neither of the teams that owned the best records in their respective leagues during the regular season — the Brewers and Rays — has won a World Series. Victory would be particularly sweet for either of those fan bases, along with the other postseason entrant without a title, the Padres.
Who will survive the gauntlet to lift the Commissioner's Trophy at the end of October? Here's when and where to watch every game.
Where to watch MLB playoffs 2026
- TV channels: Fox, FS1, TBS, NBC, NBCSN
The 2026 MLB postseason will have a new look for the opening round, with NBC carrying every wild card game on its platforms: NBC, NBCSN and/or Peacock.
After that, the familiar rotation returns. This year's NL playoffs will air on Fox or FS1 while the AL will be on TBS, with the World Series set to air on Fox as it has every year since 2000.
Fans can stream every postseason game except Peacock exclusives with DIRECTV, which offers a free trial to new subscribers.
All games airing on NBC, NBCSN, Fox and FS1 can be streamed with fubo, which also offers a free trial.

item.title: [heavy.com] Is Zack Wheeler Available? Phillies' Pitching Plan Revealed Behind Aaron Nola
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies will play in Atlanta against the Braves on Thursday night with their seasons both on the line.
It’s a decisive Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series. The teams split the first two games in the best-of-three series. Only one team can move on.
Both teams entered Thursday with a bit of uncertainty about their pitching plans, but things are beginning to take shape.
According to multiple reports, the Phillies will be starting the veteran Aaron Nola on the mound. It was the most logical decision given that he’s on full rest.
It does raise the question about Zack Wheeler, though. He hasn’t pitched in this series. Would the Phillies really go out of the postseason potentially without even using him?
There’s reason to expect that Wheeler could follow Nola at some point in Thursday’s game.
Is Zack Wheeler Available?
Wheeler is available on Thursday night, according to The Athletic’s Matt Gelb.
“Nola will be on regular rest after pitching most recently in the penultimate game of the regular season Saturday, when he opened a bullpen game on two days’ rest and only threw 21 pitches,” Gelb writes. “The Phillies could also use Zack Wheeler, who is on three days’ rest, as a reliever in Game 3. Jesús Luzardo, who started Game 1 on Tuesday, is in play for an inning or two in Game 3 if needed.”
Wheeler pitched the Phillies’ regular season finale on Sunday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Philadelphia needed to win that game to ensure a playoff spot, and they did, so Wheeler’s arm was used for a good cause there.
Generally, starting pitchers then get at least four days of rest after an outing.
If Wheeler were to pitch Thursday, he would’ve gotten three days of rest — Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
Plenty of pitchers go on shorter rest in the playoffs, but it still comes with a risk. It throws off between-start routines and has potentially a greater injury probability.
A pitcher may also be slightly less effective if their arm isn’t feeling as fresh and rested as usual.
Wheeler, though, is one of this era’s great pitchers and had a 3.00 ERA in 28 outings in the regular season for the Phillies. He’s 36 years old now and doesn’t have a ton of time left in his career, most likely. He’d be a logical guy to trust in a big spot on Thursday night.
Of course, if the Phillies were able to win without using Wheeler, he could start Game 1 of the NLDS on Saturday. But that only matters if the Phillies get there.
Zack Wheeler Short Rest History
According to John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia, Wheeler has pitched in relief on short rest once in his career.
That was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS. The Phillies were eliminated that night, 4-2, by the Diamondbacks.
Wheeler did his part, though. He went 1.2 innings out of the pen, striking out one and walking one while not allowing a hit or a run.

item.title: [New York Daily News] With dad on hand, Cody Bellinger delivers his own big Yankees moment: ‘He’s built for this’
item.dc:creator: Peter Sblendorio
item.description: The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove. In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001. But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention. item.content:encoded:
The night started with Cody Bellinger’s glove.
In a sentimental moment before Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Bellinger caught the ceremonial first pitch from his father, Clay Bellinger, who played for the Yankees from 1999-2001.
But by the end of Wednesday night, it was the younger Bellinger’s bat that commanded the attention.
Bellinger went 2-for-5 with a home run and four RBI in a 9-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx, completing a lopsided two-game sweep as the Yankees advanced to the ALDS.
“I’m able to appreciate it in the moment,” Bellinger said afterward, reflecting on sharing the night with his father. “That was a cool moment, just a great game. Happy I was able to contribute, and we’ve got a lot more work to do.”
Continued contributions from Bellinger would go a long way in the Yankees making a deep postseason run, with the AL East-winning Tampa Bay Rays up next in the ALDS.
Bellinger takes on added importance with Aaron Judge sidelined indefinitely due to a calf strain.
He was one of the driving forces in the Yankees’ two-day demolition of the archrival Red Sox, whom they outscored 18-2. The All-Star went 3-for-8 in the series and delivered a pair of key hits in Wednesday’s clincher.
With Yankees leading by a run in the fifth inning, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy controversially removed right-handed starter Sonny Gray after 70 pitches with runners at the corners and two outs.
Tracy turned to the left-handed Erik Miller to face the lefty-swinging Bellinger, who delivered an RBI single that put the Yankees up, 2-0.
Then in the sixth, after an intentional walk to Ben Rice in front of him, Bellinger capped a six-run rally with a three-run home run against right-handed reliever Garrett Whitlock — a 360-foot drive into the right-field stands that served as the dagger.
“He’s built for this,” Judge said Wednesday during a champagne-soaked celebration in the Yankees clubhouse. “He’s built for New York. He’s built for the big moment, and he continues to show up for us when we need him.”
Bellinger, who won the 2019 National League MVP and the 2020 World Series with the Los Angeles Dodgers, is in his second season with the Yankees, having re-signed last winter on a five-year, $162.5 million contract.
Despite missing a month with a hamstring strain, Bellinger batted .264 with 17 home runs, 73 RBI and a .768 OPS in 132 games. He was worth 4.6 WAR (wins above replacement), in part because of his excellent defensive work in left field, too.
“This offseason, there were a couple of other teams involved,” Clay Bellinger said in August of his son’s free agency. “But I said, ‘If you can sign back with these guys, and you go out there and you win a world championship to add to this legacy, there’s no better place in the world to play baseball.’”
The elder Bellinger would know, as the former utility player won World Series with the Yankees in 1999 and 2000.
Now, the Yankees’ World Series aspirations rest in large part with Bellinger, who continues to carve out his own pinstriped legacy.
Despite hitting left-handed, Bellinger is actually better against left-handed pitching than he is against righties, making his bat even more crucial for balance in a Judge-less lineup that’s loaded with lefties.
The Yankees went 15-for-35 (.429) against left-handers in the Red Sox series, with Bellinger recording two hits in those matchups and another top-of-the-order lefty batter in Rice totaling three.
“No secret sauce,” Bellinger said of his reverse splits. “For me, just take it as another at-bat. Felt like when I was playing baseball coming up, didn’t hear too much about the match-ups. I was just playing baseball.”
After hitting .214 in his first postseason with the Yankees, Bellinger is off to a .333 start to this one. Wednesday’s home run was Bellinger’s 11th in the postseason and his second in nine playoff games with the Yankees.
“I feel like I was able to enjoy that one,” Bellinger said. “Just a home game in Yankee Stadium, it’s a really fun atmosphere. It’s fun to play. And hopefully we get many, many more this month.”
